newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Event overload to make dealers sweat.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Event overload to make dealers sweat.

text.p: Financial markets have one of their most action-packed weeks in months coming up.
A British election, where many are gearing up for a changing of the guard, and a series of policy-sensitive U.S. economic numbers are the main events, economists said on Friday.
On top of that, markets have fallout from a weekend Group of Seven meeting and a brewing poltical battle in France, which has implications for European monetary union, on the agenda.
"The UK election is the thing that stands out in a sea of U.S. data next week," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist Yamaichi International in London.

British voters on May 1 are widely expected to ditch the Conservatives for the first time in 18 years in favour of a remodelled Labour Party. In times past this would unnerve investors but markets so far have been serene ahead of the vote.
Voter surveys have consistently shown Labour in front, usually by a large margin.
Far less predictable will be the numbers coming out of the U.S., analysts said.

There are four important sets of U.S. data -- the first-quarter employment cost index (ECI) on Tuesday, Q1 GDP on Wednesday, the April National Purchasing Management report on Thursday and, biggest of all, April payrolls on Friday.
"We have a heavy batch of data next week, coming off the back of a period of understated statistics," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
The market is going into the data anxious about the possibility of inflationary pressures and further interest rate increases.
There may be a little relief on that front, analysts said.
"Some of these numbers are going to be a little softer," Bevan said. "It could give a little boost to the Treasury market, but I would not want to bet on that."
Chester saw a similar possibility but he too was cautious.

"If the data come in surprsingly weak it would severly damange the confidence of a rate hike in May...but given the prevailing trends, I expect it to confirm the strength in the economy in Q1 and confirm the need for a further Fed tightening.
Chester said he expected the Fed to tighten by 25 basis points at the May 20 FOMC, then by a further quarter point at the following meeting on July 2.
Gwyn Hacche, senior European economist at HSBC James Capel, said, said the ECI would be key. "Given the focus of the Fed on labour costs, that could be quite important."

But Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe, said market attention would shift quickly. "It (the ECI) is not going to be dramatically bad news. Once it's over, we'll be focusing on the employment report."

Meanwhile Bevan saw French political tensions giving markets "Sentiment in France will spill over into Bunds. There might be further EMU derailment which would impact all the European markets," he said.

France, which has elections set for late May/early June, has a few key economic reports coming. Housing starts and consumer spending for March are due on Tuesday, followed by trade and unemployment on Wednesday.
President Jacques Chirac is hoping to use any signs of economic recovery as a trump card for returning his centre-right government to power.
